A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MOMEMTO and the same underlying research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, few-shot experiments, component ablations, memory sensitivity analyses, and leave-one-domain-out results.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark results and additional controlled comparisons, synthetic experiments, failure analyses, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The backbone, patch memory, gated updates, and decoder are retained. However, Appendix B.4 revises the specified computation: v4 applies softmax after selecting top-K scores and preserves the unnormalized encoder output for decoder concatenation, whereas v2's algorithms normalize across all items and overwrite the original query. These are localized algorithm revisions.

E1.justification: The 23-dataset TSB-AD-U benchmark and its 350 Eval series are retained. v4 adds synthetic reconstruction examples and controlled mean-level shifts under simple and noisy conditions in Figures 4–5, providing a limited expansion of tested input scenarios.

E2.justification: The fifteen named main-table baselines already appear in v2, despite its prose saying thirteen. v4 adds multi-domain comparison rows for existing TSFMs, evaluates UniTS and UP2ME with and without PMM in Table 5, and introduces a sequence-level-memory comparator in Table 15. These are targeted extensions of the retained comparison suite.

E3.justification: Appendix B.2 changes the stated separate-model setting from 350 individual-series models to 32 domain models, substantially revising the comparison protocol. Few-shot ratios change from extending through 90% to 80%, and v4 adds matched-window, patch-length, and runtime-scaling protocols. The detailed domain table also switches from VUS-PR to AUC-PR.

E4.justification: v4 adds sequence-versus-patch memory controls, decoder-input ablations, patch-size sensitivity, similar-window comparisons, synthetic mean-shift experiments, success/failure cases, runtime scaling, and KS score-separation analyses. These substantially expand the questions tested. The earlier leave-one-domain-out evaluation, memory-size analysis, and score-distribution plots are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v4 introduces ± values throughout the main comparison table and shaded bands in Figure 2, whereas the corresponding v2 displays contain point estimates. Table 20 explicitly reports runtime means and standard deviations over three runs. The main table's ± quantities and Figure 2's bands remain undefined, with no corresponding run count specified.

E6.justification: Many benchmark scores and few-shot curves are replaced, and numerous controlled results are added. For example, separate-model MOMEMTO AUC-PR changes from 32.83 to 34.87 under the revised training setting, so this is not a same-setting gain. The four headline multi-domain MOMEMTO scores and leave-one-domain-out results remain unchanged. Domain-level and efficiency results also change metrics or reporting conditions.

T1.justification: Section 3.1.2 corrects the memory-update and query-update attention arguments relative to v2's equations and supplies a revised formal definition of top-K retrieval weights. These are limited changes to the mathematical specification. Neither version provides theorems, proofs, or formal performance guarantees.

C1.justification: The central contribution and claimed anomaly-detection benefits remain. v4 more explicitly bounds contribution and conclusion statements to univariate detection, evaluated AUC/VUS comparisons, and few-shot improvements over MOMENT. Section 2 also adds an explicit first-attempt claim for adapting memory-guided reconstruction to TSFM-based anomaly detection.

C2.justification: v4 adds a mean-level explanation of over-generalization and discusses failures under normal distribution shifts or potentially ambiguous labels. Appendix C.5 attributes much of the gain to memory augmentation and acknowledges that the patch comparison also changes memory capacity. It also qualifies multi-domain benefits across TSFMs and specifies multivariate extension challenges.

D1.justification: v4 substantially expands reproducibility information: train-only normalization, full-series evaluation including the training segment, score aggregation, baseline fine-tuning and validation procedures, batch size, additional baseline hyperparameters, and a 0.1 memory-initialization sampling ratio. It also explains sequential memory updates, gradient handling, and fixed memory at inference. These disclosures should not all be interpreted as changed implementation settings.

R1.justification: v4 adds the UniTS and UP2ME references and expands positioning against MEMTO and H-PAD, discussing backbone initialization, memory updates, and anomaly scoring. It also makes the TSFM memory-adaptation novelty claim explicit. Most of the existing literature review and citations remain.

P1.justification: Much existing prose and the main section hierarchy are retained. v4 changes the title and TFM/TSFM terminology, revises introductory and methodological passages, expands procedural explanations, moves computational-efficiency discussion to Appendix C.9, and reorders appendix subsections. These editorial changes are limited relative to the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v4 redraws Figure 1, revises the few-shot plot, converts the retrieval-sensitivity chart into a table, adds a notation table and numerous experimental displays, and restructures the efficiency table. Journal typography, headers, and page layout change throughout. The original score-distribution and memory-utilization images are retained despite relocation or renumbering.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the central mechanism through sequence-memory and decoder controls, similar-window comparisons, and synthetic and real failure analyses that v2 lacked. Expanded algorithm and evaluation documentation also improves reproducibility. These gains clarify what memory contributes and where it fails, rather than merely reporting higher scores. Undefined main-result uncertainty displays and the capacity-confounded memory comparison remain limitations, but the overall improvement is substantial.
